events.name: ISAW Exhibition Lecture: Cursing, Curing, Creating: The Culture of Magic in Ancient Egypt
events.description: Foy ScalfInstitute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, University of Chicago For the ancient Egyptians, magic was not an illicit alternative to religion or a mysterious violation of the natural world. Heka—the force usually translated as “magic”—was woven into creation itself and provided gods and humans with the causative power to make things happen. Drawing on texts and objects featured in the ISAW exhibition Cursed! The Power of Magic in the Ancient World, this lecture explores how Egyptians used spoken spells, written words, images, amulets, ritual actions, and sacred substances to heal the sick, protect children, defeat enemies, communicate with the dead, and transform their spirits.  This lecture will take place in person at ISAW (15 East 84th Street).

events.description: In conjunction with the Grey Art Museum’s exhibition by Alison Knowles: A Retrospective (1960–2022), on view from Sept. 9, 2026–Jan. 20, 2027. Join Prof. André Lepecki and Prof. Jeannine Tang (Department of Performance Studies, NYU Tisch) for a lunchtime conversation catalyzed by Alison Knowles’s performance The Identical Lunch, based on the artist’s habitual order at NYC diner Riss Foods: “a tuna fish sandwich on wheat toast with butter and lettuce, no mayo, and a cup of soup or glass of buttermilk.” From 1969 until the artist’s death in 2025, numerous artists, friends, and strangers ate variations of this lunch with Knowles across the United States and internationally, writing about their experiences as performers and documentarians of this iconic work. Honoring this legacy, discussion will situate the performance within Knowles’s art of everyday life, ritual, and relation. It will also consider the implications of posthumously activating this communal performance, including changing food cultures such as the recent viral spread of the humble tuna fish sandwich. Attendees will dine on Knowles’s signature meal, and vegan alternatives will be available.

events.name: Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet Virtual Talkback and Film Screening
events.description: Virtual post-screening discussion and Q&A with French director Matthieu Verdeil and distinguished scholar Dr. Robert Reid-Pharr. This program is organized by the Center for Black Visual Culture and co-sponsored by NYU Institute of French Studies and NYU Department of Social and Cultural Analysis. Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet (52’ - 2025 - english subtitles) film will be shared to all registrants via email with a viewing link, 48 hours in advance of the program. After 48 hours, the film will no longer be available to view. To have access to the film viewing link you must register BEFORE November 27th. Claude McKay, Wanderings of a Rebellious Poet is a captivating voyage through the 1920s — from Harlem to Marseille, via Jamaica, Russia and Morocco — in the footsteps of Jamaican American writer Claude McKay. A rebellious voice of the Harlem Renaissance, Claude McKay spent two decades traveling the world, immersing himself in artistic and political avant-gardes while building an enduring body of work. This remarkable documentary portrait, illustrated with rare archival footage and photographs, narrated by Gaël Faye, and set to a stirring soundtrack, brings his legacy to life. For over 20 years, film director and producer Matthieu Verdeil has pursued a distinctive path at the crossroads of history, memory, and artistic creation. He collaborates with contemporary artists such as Abraham Poincheval while dedicating much of his career to rediscovering overlooked figures and movements in cultural history, including Varian Fry and Claude McKay. Verdeil first became interested in McKay in the early 2000s, recognizing him as both a pioneer of the Harlem Renaissance and a forerunner of global Black consciousness. He began extensive archival research, working with U.S. scholars Brent Hayes Edwards and French publisher Renaud Boukh (Héliotropismes). In 2021, Verdeil directed Claude McKay: From Harlem to Marseille, the first documentary devoted to the “vagabond poet.” Combining historical rigor with poetic sensitivity, the film was screened in France, the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom and beyond. Currently, Verdeil is preparing a new television film dedicated to the Harlem Renaissance, continuing his long-standing commitment to amplifying forgotten or marginalized voices whose legacies continue to shape our present, and to exploring the transatlantic fabric of Black thought. Robert F. Reid-Pharr is a Professor of Social and Cultural Analysis at New York University. He holds a Ph.D. in American Studies and an M.A. in African American Studies from Yale University as well as a B.A. in Political Science from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He has been the Jess and Sara Cloud Distinguished Visiting Professor of English at the College of William and Mary, the Edward Said Visiting Chair of American Studies at the American University of Beirut, the Drue Heinz Visiting Professor of English at the University of Oxford, the Carlisle and Barbara Moore Distinguished Visiting Professor of English at the University of Oregon, and the F.O. Matthiessen Visiting Professor of Gender and Sexuality at Harvard University. A prominent scholar in the field of race and sexuality studies, he is the author of four books and numerous essays. His research and writing have been supported by grants from the Mellon Foundation, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Studies, and the American Academy in Berlin. His work has been honored by the Publishing Triangle, the Modern Language Association and the American Literature Association. In 2015 he was inducted into the Johns Hopkins Society of Scholars and he is the recipient of a 2016 John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship.

events.name: ISAW Lecture: “Reconsidering the Rise of a Newly Discovered Iron Age Kingdom in Anatolia: Great King Hartapu and the Türkmen-Karahöyük Archaeological Project”
events.description: James Osborne University of Chicago Since the 2019 discovery of a royal inscription authored by “Great King Hartapu,” Iron Age Anatolian scholarship has been energised by the appearance of a hitherto unknown kingdom in the Konya Plain. While the historical context of Hartapu’s inscriptions have undergone dramatic reassessment in light of this new text, little attention has been paid to the conditions that would have contributed to the rise of this kingdom in the first place. This lecture proposes several factors that likely played a role in the emergence of the kingdom: cultural and economic interaction with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, similar relations with Phrygia, emulative competition with its local peer polities and a propitious ecological setting at a time of significant environmental transformations. This lecture will take place in person at ISAW (15 East 84th Street).

events.name: Tracing the Politics of Migration from Ottoman Syria through US Emp
events.description:
<p>Join the Middle East Institute and the Center for the Study of Ethnicity and Race for a book talk with Randa Tawil about her book, <em>Race in Transit:The Politics of Migration from Ottoman Syria through US Empire</em><strong>.&nbsp;</strong>At the turn of the twentieth century, life in Ottoman Syria was upended by European and US colonial and capital expansion. Many people responded by migrating to the United States. In doing so, they stepped into the world of international migration, where they had to navigate overlapping states and migration infrastructures&mdash;shipping companies and ticketing agents, health inspectors and border police, universities and kinship networks&mdash;that each facilitated, restricted, and policed movement.&nbsp;In this&nbsp;book, Randa Tawil&nbsp;follows the itineraries of the early Syrian diaspora, stitching together migrants&#39; travels across archives from Beirut, Marseille, Liverpool, Manila, Washington, D.C., Michigan, and Texas. She reveals the overlapping and contradicting ways in which race was forged globally in the early twentieth century and its effects on Syrians in the United States. Syrian migrants encountered multiple imperial and national legal regimes during transit, and their varying relationships with different empires set the conditions under which migrants were considered &quot;desirable&quot; or &quot;undesirable&quot; once they reached US borders. Focusing on the experiences of those on the move, <em>Race in Transit</em> makes migrants the agents of a world history that has too often relegated them to the sidelines.</p>
<p>Randa Tawil is an author, researcher, and lecturer at the University of Washington in Seattle. Her research explores the intersections of migration policing, imperial expansion, and their constructions of race, gender, and sexuality. Her first book, <em>Race in Transit: The Politics of Migration from Ottoman Syria through US Empire,&nbsp;</em>published through Stanford University Press, reveals how infrastructures of migration form the desirability&nbsp;of migrants for accepting states. Her work has appeared&nbsp;in Open Democracy, the Washington Post, Ottoman History Podcast, and Margins, as well as numerous academic journals.&nbsp;</p>

events.name: Finding Merging SMBHs with Time-Domain Surveys
events.description: Inspiraling  supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs), expected products of galaxy mergers and strong low-frequency gravitational-wave sources, are difficult to resolve at sub-parsec scales. Their orbits may instead be traced through periodic or chirping AGN variability, including relativistic Doppler boosting. I will present optical-survey methods combining accretion-flow models with Bayesian chirp detection. My results suggest that mixtures of mini-disk and circumbinary-disk emission are present in observations by Rubin’s LSST. In PTF, a Bayesian chirp-plus-noise search finds 33 apparent multi-cycle fits among 35,383 quasars, but none remains phase-coherent with extended ASAS-SN and ZTF data. Ten-year LSST simulations recover chirps across broad merger-time and amplitude ranges under the assumed models. However, mini-disks may be more visible in UV/X-rays for many systems considered, motivating broad, deep surveys to probe more binary parameter space.

events.name: Predicting the dark matter - baryon abundance ratio
events.description: We discuss relaxation solutions to the dark matter - baryon coincidence problem in the context of QCD axion dark matter. In relaxation solutions, a moduli dynamically adjusts the mass of dark matter and baryons until their energy densities are O(1) the same. Because the QCD axion is heavily connected to QCD, scanning the QCD axion mass inherently also scans the proton mass. In the context of relaxation solutions, this implies that the ratio of dark matter to baryon abundances (ΩDM/ΩB) is a ratio of beta functions showing that these models can only accommodate discrete values of ΩDM/ΩB thereby “predicting” the ratio of the dark matter to baryon abundances. The original composite axion model has only a single integer degree of freedom N, the size of the gauge group, and we show that when N = 8 the observed value of ΩDM/ΩB = 5.36 is reproduced to within its percent level error bars. Novel tests of this model include more precise measurements of ΩDM/ΩB, a better lattice determination of the dependence of the proton mass on the high energy QCD gauge coupling, as well as more traditional tests such as fifth force experiments.

events.name: Nanosecond Optical Techniques for Imaging and Measurement in the Brain
events.description: Fluorescence lifetime imaging is a promising approach for quantitative measurement of biological signals. We present recent progress developing fast optical methods to image nanosecond fluorescence lifetimes. Electro-optic fluorescence lifetime imaging (EO-FLIM) uses polarization modulators to gate images onto standard scientific cameras, allowing lifetime estimation at every image pixel in parallel with high photon throughput. We demonstrate that EO-FLIM may be applied to wide-field imaging of genetically encoded voltage indicators expressed in the brains of awake, behaving animals, achieving picosecond lifetime resolution and kilohertz frame rates. Action potentials and subthreshold voltage dynamics are resolved in lifetime and are mapped throughout neuronal structures. Intensity noise from motion, hemodynamics, and speckle is strongly suppressed. Standard techniques rely on measuring ΔF/F to quantify neuronal activity. EO-FLIM instead measures absolute changes in fluorescence lifetime without normalization to a moving average, pointing toward future calibrated voltage measurements in the brain. We also explore nanosecond time as a resource for multiplexing to speed up volumetric imaging and to enable simultaneous measurement of multiple fluorescent sensors.

events.name: Collective Phenomena in Superconducting Circuits: From Giant Atoms to Dissipative Time Crystals
events.description: Superconducting circuits empower artificial atoms and photonic lattices with engineered geometries, interactions, and dissipation, providing an excellent platform for exploring light–matter interactions and collective nonequilibrium dynamics. A giant atom can be formed by coupling a transmon to a waveguide at multiple points separated on the wavelength scale. We investigate two giant atoms in a nested configuration using complex transmission spectroscopy to characterize frequency-dependent individual radiative decay, collective decay, and coherent exchange, arising from interference between coupling points. These measurements provide a basis for exploring photon correlations and dissipative preparation of entangled states. We also realize a nonlinear bosonic Kitaev chain in the synthetic frequency dimension of a superconducting multimode cavity, with parametrically controlled hopping and pairing interactions. Above the parametric instability threshold, Kerr frequency shifts limit photon-number growth. The interplay of driving, nonlinearity, and photon loss produces stationary and self-sustained oscillatory regimes controlled by the gauge-invariant coupling phase and detuning. Steady-state emission spectra and temporal correlations provide evidence for dissipative time-crystalline behavior; quench experiments distinguish the emergent oscillation frequency from preparation-dependent transients.

events.name: Origins of THz Radiation from Ultrafast Light-driven Ferromagnets and Antiferromagnetic Mott Insulators
events.description:
The ultrafast demagnetization is a surprising phenomenon discovered in 1996 in which a femtosecond laser pulse (fsLP) pumping of a ferromagnet leads to its demagnetization, as nonclassical dynamics where magnetization vector is shrinking in length while not rotating. Despite being one of the primary experimental observables, THz electromagnetic radiation from either a single magnetic layer, or much more enhanced from ferromagnet/spin-orbit-material bilayers [1], has rarely been calculated. This has forced experimentalists to develop intuitive pictures [1], such as of interlayer spin current generated by “spin voltage” that is converted into charge currents via spin-orbit coupling induced mechanisms. events.name: Controlling Buried Interfaces in Epitaxial Quantum Materials.
events.description: Epitaxial interfaces often determine the structural and electronic properties of quantum materials, particularly when multiple interactions compete or when chemically dissimilar materials are combined. In this talk, I will discuss two examples in which the buried interface plays a central role in the resulting behavior. First, I will describe remote epitaxy frustration of GdAuGe on graphene/SiC, where the growing film experiences competing periodic potentials from both graphene and the underlying substrate. By tuning the graphene–substrate coupling, we find an intermediate regime in which the interface loses long-range translational order while retaining local atomic order. This structurally frustrated interface exhibits a magnetic response consistent with a strong interfacial contribution, with signatures persisting to room temperature. Second, I will discuss the growth of FeSe on GaAs, where direct integration is limited by interfacial reactions and secondary-phase formation. I will show a low-temperature growth window around 200 °C that suppresses these reactions while maintaining crystalline FeSe and discuss an ultrathin Bi interlayer as a route toward interfacial spin–orbit engineering. Taken together, these studies highlight how buried interfaces can give rise to unexpected structural and magnetic behavior, while also providing a means to control heterogeneous integration in epitaxial quantum materials.

events.name: Inference through Compression: Learning the Physics of Multicomponent Systems
events.description: Physical understanding benefits from simplicity and interpretability, yet quantitative prediction in complex systems often demands much richer descriptions. In this talk, I will show how compression can be used to extract physical insights from systems in which the microscopic details still matter quantitatively. Using examples drawn from heteropolymers, biomolecular systems, and programmable soft matter, I will demonstrate that the thermodynamic structure of multicomponent systems can itself be compressed, so that molecules acquire low-dimensional representations through their interactions with other components. These representations retain the relevant physical information while enabling quantitatively accurate predictions of thermodynamic properties across a wide range of mixtures and conditions. By revealing which microscopic details control collective behavior, this approach provides a systematic route to infer effective variables, extrapolate to new systems and conditions, and rationally design multicomponent matter.

events.name: Quantum Printing
events.description:
I  introduce Quantum Printing- a concept for controlling quantum matter by directly imprinting the quantum numbers carried by structured light (spin angular momentum, orbital angular momentum, chirality, and entanglement) onto coherent electron and magnetic states. Structured light acts as a quantum “ink” that writes, manipulates, and erases macroscopic quantum orders in both charged fluids (superconductors and quantum Hall systems) and neutral fluids (magnets), going beyond conventional thermal or magnetic control.
I will also introduce extensions of these ideas to reversible optical writing and erasing of topological skyrmions in Heisenberg magnets with THz structured beams, enabling error-corrected magnetic memory, sub-diffraction patterning, and calligraphy of continuous textures [2].Work supported by DOE DE-SC-0025580, ERC-2018-SYG 810451 HERO, KAW 2019.0068.[1]

events.name: How Dust Evolution Shapes Protoplanetary Disks
events.description:
"    Planet formation begins with the coagulation of micrometer-sized dust grains in a protoplanetary disk. This particle growth not only provides the building material for planetesimals but also shapes the environments they form in. 
    Aerodynamic drag forces between gas and dust determine how fast the grains drift and how efficiently they can be trapped in the frequently observed rings and vortices in protoplanetary disks. The size of the particles thus affects the available dust mass and composition throughout the disk. Dust also dominates the opacities and therefore regulates the thermal structure and the onset of hydrodynamic instabilities that depend on thermal relaxation. 
In my talk, I will present two recent applications of coupled multifluid simulations and dust coagulation models that capture the interplay of microphysics and large-scale dynamics in protoplanetary disks: 
    Our simulations of planet-disk systems with dust coagulation quantify the amount of small dust grains that diffuse and drift through planet-induced gaps. These calculations constrain the composition and available mass of solids in the inner disk regions.
    We furthermore investigate the effects of dust evolution on protoplanetary disk turbulence, induced by the Vertical Shear Instability. Our simulations show that efficient dust coagulation can suppress turbulence in protoplanetary disks, due to the reduced collisional cooling in the dust-depleted upper layers.
    Understanding how dust coagulation influences the dynamics of protoplanetary disks is thus key to understanding the initial conditions for planet formation and to interpreting multi-wavelength observations."

events.name: AI-Assisted Physics Research: Experiences and Caveats
events.description: In this talk, I will share my experiences of using AI in theoretical physics research. I will first discuss how the AI chatbox can help understand and push forward a project under human's control. Then, I will discuss how AI agents work, from giving them specific calculation tasks to asking them to explore a vague research idea. I will discuss some difficulties I encountered during this AI-assisted workflow. In particular, sometimes the agent moved away from the physical setting of the project, or continued developing an argument before I understood the previous steps. Based on these experiences, I will discuss how to better work with AI, check its results, and keep track of the direction of a research project. The focus will be on practical research experience rather than the technical details of AI, so no prior knowledge of AI is needed.

events.name: Using Tidal Disruption Events as Probes of Massive Black Hole Formation and Growth Over Cosmic Time
events.description: The tidal disruption of a star that wanders too close to a central black hole is a unique probe of quiescent supermassive black holes lurking in the nuclei of galaxies.  We have demonstrated the ability to discover and spectroscopically classify large samples of tidal disruption events (TDEs) in the optical from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) Northern Sky Survey, with systematic high-energy follow-up with Swift and XMM-Newton. From these efforts, we now know the spectroscopic signatures, multi-wavelength properties, and host galaxy preferences of TDEs, and can begin to use TDEs as powerful probes of massive black hole demographics in quiescent galaxies.  One of the most exciting applications of TDEs is the ability to probe intermediate mass black holes (IMBHs) that are expected to reside in dwarf galaxies, with demographics that encode the seeding mechanism of massive black holes in the early Universe.  I will outline our strategy in the next decade for searching for TDEs across the black hole mass function, and over cosmic time, by extending our sensitivity to TDEs to lower central black hole masses and higher redshifts, by exploiting the discovery power of the next generation of wide-field time domain surveys, including Rubin, Roman, ULTRASAT, and UVEX.

events.name: A Hierarchy of Exact Lower Bounds on the Laughlin Spectral Gap: a Bootstrap Approach
events.description: Although the Laughlin state's ability to qualitatively describe many aspects of the fractional quantum Hall effect has long been clear, a rigorous proof that the parent Hamiltonian (the first Haldane pseudopotential) has a spectral gap in the thermodynamic limit has remained open for over four decades. In this talk, we will discuss our recently developed bootstrap approach to deriving positive lower bounds for the spectral gap on the sphere for arbitrary $N_\Phi$ including in the thermodynamic limit $N_\Phi \to \infty$ [1,2]. Our approach can in principle be generalized to pseudopotentials describing other model wavefunctions such as the Moore--Read state or Read--Rezayi sequence. More generally, this work demonstrates that bootstrap methods can be used to rigorously resolve major open problems in quantum many-body physics.[1] M. G. Scheer, E. Khalaf arXiv:2610.18854 (2026)[2] The Laughlin gap problem was also recently solved in a paper by OpenAI. We emphasize that our work is independent and in many ways preceded the OpenAI result and we will discuss the similarities and differences between the two approaches.

events.name: Emulating the Bose-Hubbard Model with Arrays of Superconducting Qubits
events.description: In this talk, we study the propagation, entanglement, and entropy of quantum information using 3x3 and 4x4 arrays of superconducting qubits that emulate the two-dimensional (2D) hard-core Bose-Hubbard model. events.name: Stochastic Dualities in Active Matter
events.description: First-passage processes and stationary states are traditionally regarded as distinct aspects of stochastic dynamics, governed by the backward and forward evolution equations, respectively. In this seminar, I will discuss how the backward equation can be reinterpreted as the forward equation of a dual stochastic process. This introduces a dual system whose stationary observables can be directly related to first-passage quantities of the original system.I will first discuss the application of this duality formalism to active matter under wall confinement. Using the duality relation, I will show how dynamic adsorption of active particles at confining walls directly encodes splitting probabilities, revealing dynamic adsorption and first-passage properties as complementary manifestations of directional persistence.In the second part of the talk, I will shift from boundary confinement to bulk transport by applying the same duality formalism to effective diffusion in periodic force fields. I will show how the effective diffusion coefficient can be expressed entirely in terms of stationary distributions of the physical and dual systems, providing a new perspective on transport in periodic nonequilibrium systems.

events.name: Exhibition Lecture: Cursing, Curing, Creating: The Culture of Magic in Ancient Egypt
events.description:
Speaker: Foy Scalf

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. For the ancient Egyptians, magic was not an illicit alternative to religion or a mysterious violation of the natural world. Heka—the force usually translated as “magic”—was woven into creation itself and provided gods and humans with the causative power to make things happen. Drawing on texts and objects featured in the ISAW exhibition Cursed! The Power of Magic in the Ancient World, this lecture explores how Egyptians used spoken spells, written words, images, amulets, ritual actions, and sacred substances to heal the sick, protect children, defeat enemies, communicate with the dead, and transform their spirits. Seen from an Egyptian perspective, cursing, curing, and creating were not separate domains but different expressions of a world in which magic was an expected part of everyday life.

events.name: Overseas Trade and its Impact on a New Ruling Class in China at the Turn of the First Millenium CE
events.description:
Speaker: Gregory Sattler

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. China’s Song dynasty (960–1279) began as a military government ruling a population devastated by decades of civil war following one of the most tumultuous periods of Chinese history. Yet, the Song dynasty was merely only the latest in a series of short-lived dynasties that attempted to rule China. Its leaders understood that their predecessors failed because they succumbed to the instability of military rule, and thus a balance was sought in which a greatly expanded civil bureaucracy could offset the monopoly of power held by military men.

Picturing Ancient People: Gender in Ancient Greek Vase-Painting

This workshop will take place online. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Zoom information will be provided via confirmation email to registered participants. events.name: Exhibition Lecture: Portable Prayers: Objects, Adornment, and Devotion in Jewish Antiquity
events.description:
Speaker: Karen Stern

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Conventional studies of ancient Jewish prayer and its evolution focus primarily on recitations or performances of precatory texts, liturgy, or poetry once conducted inside Jewish homes, synagogues, and study halls. This talk adopts a different focus: it considers inextricable connections between the minds, hearts, and bodies of Jewish supplicants and the portable things that they once attached to their bodies with strings and cords, including inscribed amulets and phylacteries of various sorts.

events.name: Reconsidering the Rise of a Newly Discovered Iron Age Kingdom in Anatolia:
events.description:
Speaker: James Osborne

Great King Hartapu and the Türkmen-Karahöyük Archaeological Project

This lecture will take place in person at ISAW. Registration is required; click through for the registration link. Since the 2019 discovery of a royal inscription authored by "Great King Hartapu," Iron Age Anatolian scholarship has been energised by the appearance of a hitherto unknown kingdom in the Konya Plain. While the historical context of Hartapu’s inscriptions have undergone dramatic reassessment in light of this new text, little attention has been paid to the conditions that would have contributed to the rise of this kingdom in the first place. This lecture proposes several factors that likely played a role in the emergence of the kingdom: cultural and economic interaction with the Neo-Assyrian Empire, similar relations with Phrygia, emulative competition with its local peer polities and a propitious ecological setting at a time of significant environmental transformations.
